exercises.title: Movies per decade
exercises.task: Count the movies released in each decade from 1950 to 1999. A decade is the year rounded down to a multiple of 10 (1950, 1960 …).
exercises.hint: intDiv(year, 10) * 10 gives the decade.
exercises.solution:
SELECT intDiv(year, 10) * 10 AS decade, count() AS movies
FROM imdb.movies
WHERE year BETWEEN 1950 AND 1999
GROUP BY decade
ORDER BY decade

exercises.title: Busiest towns in 2022
exercises.task: Find the 5 towns with the most property sales in 2022.
exercises.hint: toYear(date) = 2022, then ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 5.
exercises.solution:
SELECT town, count() AS sales
FROM uk.uk_price_paid
WHERE toYear(date) = 2022
GROUP BY town
ORDER BY sales DESC, town
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Top genres since 2000
exercises.task: Join movies to their genres and find the 5 genres with the most movies released in 2000 or later.
exercises.hint: movies_genres.movie_id = movies.id
exercises.solution:
SELECT g.genre, count() AS movies
FROM imdb.movies_genres AS g
INNER JOIN imdb.movies AS m ON m.id = g.movie_id
WHERE m.year >= 2000
GROUP BY g.genre
ORDER BY movies DESC, g.genre
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Most active Hacker News authors
exercises.task: Run this one in the browser playground. Find the 5 authors (column by) who posted the most stories in 2020, with their average story score. Only count rows where type = 'story' and the author is not empty.
exercises.hint: `by` is a reserved word in SQL, so quote it with backticks or alias it.
exercises.solution:
SELECT `by` AS author, count() AS stories, round(avg(score), 2) AS avg_score
FROM hackernews.hackernews
WHERE type = 'story' AND toYear(time) = 2020 AND `by` != ''
GROUP BY author
ORDER BY stories DESC, author
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Airlines with the most flights
exercises.task: Run this one in the browser playground. For 2019, find the 5 airlines (Reporting_Airline) with the most flights (all rows), and the average arrival delay (ArrDelay) of their flights that were neither cancelled nor diverted. A cancelled flight has ArrDelay = 0, so leaving those rows in would make airlines look more punctual than they are.
exercises.hint: Filter on Year, the first column of the table's sort key, so ClickHouse skips the other years. avgIf(ArrDelay, Cancelled = 0 AND Diverted = 0) averages only the flights that arrived.
exercises.solution:
SELECT Reporting_Airline AS airline, count() AS flights,
       round(avgIf(ArrDelay, Cancelled = 0 AND Diverted = 0), 2) AS avg_arr_delay
FROM ontime.ontime
WHERE Year = 2019
GROUP BY airline
ORDER BY flights DESC
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Median London price
exercises.task: For town LONDON, return the exact median sale price for each year from 2018 to 2022.
exercises.hint: median() is approximate. Use quantileExact(0.5)(price) to get the exact value.
exercises.solution:
SELECT toYear(date) AS year, quantileExact(0.5)(price) AS median_price
FROM uk.uk_price_paid
WHERE town = 'LONDON' AND year BETWEEN 2018 AND 2022
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year

exercises.title: Most expensive street per year
exercises.task: For town MANCHESTER, show each year from 2019 to 2022 with the highest sale price and the street of that sale, without a JOIN or subquery.
exercises.hint: argMax(street, price) returns the street of the row with the highest price.
exercises.solution:
SELECT toYear(date) AS year, max(price) AS max_price, argMax(street, price) AS street
FROM uk.uk_price_paid
WHERE town = 'MANCHESTER' AND year BETWEEN 2019 AND 2022
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year

exercises.title: Taxi trips by weekday
exercises.task: For every day of the week (1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday), return the number of trips, the average trip distance and the percentage of trips paid by card (payment_type = 'CRE').
exercises.cols: day_of_week, trips, avg_distance, card_pct (both rounded to 2 decimals)
exercises.hint: countIf(condition) counts only the matching rows, so you don't need a CASE inside sum().
exercises.solution:
SELECT
    toDayOfWeek(pickup_datetime) AS day_of_week,
    count() AS trips,
    round(avg(trip_distance), 2) AS avg_distance,
    round(countIf(payment_type = 'CRE') / count() * 100, 2) AS card_pct
FROM nyc_taxi.trips
GROUP BY day_of_week
ORDER BY day_of_week

exercises.title: COVID in Bosnia and Herzegovina
exercises.task: Run this one in the browser playground. For location_key = 'BA', sum new confirmed cases and new deaths per year.
exercises.hint: The new_* columns are daily values; the cumulative_* columns are running totals. Sum the daily ones.
exercises.solution:
SELECT toYear(date) AS year, sum(new_confirmed) AS confirmed, sum(new_deceased) AS deceased
FROM covid.covid19
WHERE location_key = 'BA'
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year

exercises.title: Genres as one string
exercises.task: For the movies with ids 267038 (Pulp Fiction), 207992 (The Matrix) and 333856 (Titanic, 1997), return each movie's genres as one alphabetically sorted, comma-separated string, for example Crime, Drama.
exercises.hint: groupArray collects values into an array, arraySort sorts it, and arrayStringConcat(arr, ', ') joins it.
exercises.solution:
SELECT m.name, m.year, arrayStringConcat(arraySort(groupArray(g.genre)), ', ') AS genres
FROM imdb.movies AS m
INNER JOIN imdb.movies_genres AS g ON g.movie_id = m.id
WHERE m.id IN (267038, 207992, 333856)
GROUP BY m.name, m.year
ORDER BY m.year, m.name

exercises.title: Partitioned readings table
exercises.task: Create a database practice and a table practice.readings_m with the same columns as meters.readings. Use the MergeTree engine, partition it by month (toYYYYMM(ts)) and order it by (meter_id, ts). Insert all readings of meters 1 to 10. Then run the check query and paste its result.
exercises.hint: Write the CREATE TABLE yourself; don't use CREATE TABLE … AS. Run SHOW CREATE TABLE meters.readings if you need a reference.
exercises.verify:
SELECT partition, sum(rows) AS rows
FROM system.parts
WHERE database = 'practice' AND table = 'readings_m' AND active
GROUP BY partition
ORDER BY partition
exercises.solution:
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS practice;
CREATE DATABASE practice;
CREATE TABLE practice.readings_m
(
    meter_id    UInt32,
    ts          DateTime('UTC'),
    value       Decimal(12, 3),
    ingested_at DateTime('UTC')
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts)
ORDER BY (meter_id, ts);
INSERT INTO practice.readings_m SELECT * FROM meters.readings WHERE meter_id BETWEEN 1 AND 10;

-- check query
SELECT partition, sum(rows) AS rows
FROM system.parts
WHERE database = 'practice' AND table = 'readings_m' AND active
GROUP BY partition
ORDER BY partition

exercises.title: Materialized local date
exercises.task: Add a column local_date Date to practice.readings_m that ClickHouse computes automatically as the reading's date in the Europe/Sarajevo time zone. Then fill it for the existing rows. Run the check query and paste its result. The 29th has 4 readings fewer (one hour) because the clocks move forward that night.
exercises.hint: ADD COLUMN … MATERIALIZED toDate(ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo'), then ALTER TABLE … MATERIALIZE COLUMN local_date.
exercises.verify:
SELECT local_date, count() AS readings
FROM practice.readings_m
WHERE meter_id = 6 AND local_date BETWEEN '2026-03-28' AND '2026-03-30'
GROUP BY local_date
ORDER BY local_date
exercises.solution:
ALTER TABLE practice.readings_m ADD COLUMN local_date Date MATERIALIZED toDate(ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo');
ALTER TABLE practice.readings_m MATERIALIZE COLUMN local_date SETTINGS mutations_sync = 1;

-- check query
SELECT local_date, count() AS readings
FROM practice.readings_m
WHERE meter_id = 6 AND local_date BETWEEN '2026-03-28' AND '2026-03-30'
GROUP BY local_date
ORDER BY local_date

exercises.title: Drop a month
exercises.task: The January data has to be reloaded. Remove all of January 2026 from practice.readings_m in one instant operation, without using DELETE. Run the check query and paste its result.
exercises.hint: ALTER TABLE … DROP PARTITION <partition id>. Exercise 11 showed you the partition ids.
exercises.verify:
SELECT min(ts) AS first_ts, count() AS rows
FROM practice.readings_m
exercises.solution:
ALTER TABLE practice.readings_m DROP PARTITION 202601;

-- check query
SELECT min(ts) AS first_ts, count() AS rows
FROM practice.readings_m

exercises.title: Delete and update rows
exercises.task: Do two fixes on practice.readings_m: (1) delete all readings of meter 5 on the UTC date 2026-02-01; (2) every reading that arrived more than 1 day late should get ingested_at = ts + 10 minutes. Run the check query and paste its result.
exercises.hint: Use a lightweight DELETE FROM … WHERE for the delete and ALTER TABLE … UPDATE … WHERE for the update. Check system.mutations to see when the update has finished.
exercises.verify:
SELECT
    countIf(meter_id = 5 AND toDate(ts) = '2026-02-01') AS meter5_feb1_left,
    countIf(ingested_at > ts + INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS late_left,
    count() AS rows
FROM practice.readings_m
exercises.solution:
DELETE FROM practice.readings_m WHERE meter_id = 5 AND toDate(ts) = '2026-02-01';
ALTER TABLE practice.readings_m UPDATE ingested_at = ts + INTERVAL 10 MINUTE WHERE ingested_at > ts + INTERVAL 1 DAY SETTINGS mutations_sync = 1;

-- check query
SELECT
    countIf(meter_id = 5 AND toDate(ts) = '2026-02-01') AS meter5_feb1_left,
    countIf(ingested_at > ts + INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS late_left,
    count() AS rows
FROM practice.readings_m

exercises.title: Deduplicating table
exercises.task: The meter feed sometimes sends the same reading twice, and the later copy is the correct one. Create practice.readings_dedup with an engine that keeps only the row with the newest ingested_at for each (meter_id, ts). Insert all of meters.readings into it. Run the check query and paste its result.
exercises.hint: ReplacingMergeTree(ingested_at) ORDER BY (meter_id, ts). Merges happen in the background, so read with FINAL to get exact results.
exercises.verify:
SELECT count() AS rows, sum(value) AS total_value
FROM practice.readings_dedup FINAL
exercises.solution:
CREATE TABLE practice.readings_dedup
(
    meter_id    UInt32,
    ts          DateTime('UTC'),
    value       Decimal(12, 3),
    ingested_at DateTime('UTC')
)
ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(ingested_at)
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts)
ORDER BY (meter_id, ts);
INSERT INTO practice.readings_dedup SELECT * FROM meters.readings;

-- check query
SELECT count() AS rows, sum(value) AS total_value
FROM practice.readings_dedup FINAL

exercises.title: Dataset inventory
exercises.task: Start every new dataset with an overview. Per utility, return the number of meters that sent readings, the number of reading rows, and the first and last reading time.
exercises.hint: Join readings to meters on meter_id, then use uniqExact(meter_id), count(), min(ts) and max(ts).
exercises.solution:
SELECT m.utility, uniqExact(r.meter_id) AS meters, count() AS readings, min(r.ts) AS first_ts, max(r.ts) AS last_ts
FROM meters.readings AS r
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = r.meter_id
GROUP BY m.utility
ORDER BY m.utility

exercises.title: Daily consumption of one meter
exercises.task: A day's consumption is the last register value of that day minus the last register value of the previous day. For meter 1, return the consumption of each UTC day from 2026-01-05 to 2026-01-11. If a timestamp has several rows, use the one with the newest ingested_at.
exercises.hint: argMax(value, (ts, ingested_at)) gives the last value of the day. Include January 4 in the inner query so January 5 has a previous day, and filter it out at the end. On the first row, lagInFrame returns 0 rather than NULL, so January 4 would show the whole register value; that is another reason to drop it.
exercises.solution:
SELECT day, kwh
FROM
(
    SELECT day, day_end - lagInFrame(day_end) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS kwh
    FROM
    (
        SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, argMax(value, (ts, ingested_at)) AS day_end
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id = 1 AND ts >= '2026-01-04' AND ts < '2026-01-12'
        GROUP BY day
    )
)
WHERE day >= '2026-01-05'
ORDER BY day

exercises.title: Monthly consumption per utility
exercises.task: Use the simple method: for each meter and each UTC month, consumption = max(value) − min(value). Then sum the meters per utility. Use the raw readings (no deduplication) and leave out meters 42, 99 and 230, which have known problems you will handle in module 5.
exercises.cols: month (first day of the month, e.g. 2026-01-01), utility, consumption (rounded to 2 decimals)
exercises.hint: Aggregate per (month, meter_id) in a subquery, then join to meters.meters and aggregate again per (month, utility).
exercises.solution:
SELECT t.month, m.utility, round(sum(t.consumption), 2) AS consumption
FROM
(
    SELECT toStartOfMonth(ts) AS month, meter_id, max(value) - min(value) AS consumption
    FROM meters.readings
    WHERE meter_id NOT IN (42, 99, 230)
    GROUP BY month, meter_id
) AS t
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = t.meter_id
GROUP BY t.month, m.utility
ORDER BY t.month, m.utility

exercises.title: Top electricity customers
exercises.task: Find the 5 customers who used the most electricity in February 2026 (UTC). Use the same max − min method per meter, add up all of a customer's electricity meters, and leave out meters 42, 99 and 230.
exercises.hint: Some customers have two electricity meters, so add them up per customer.
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id AS customer_id, c.name AS name, round(sum(t.kwh), 2) AS kwh
FROM
(
    SELECT meter_id, max(value) - min(value) AS kwh
    FROM meters.readings
    WHERE ts >= '2026-02-01' AND ts < '2026-03-01' AND meter_id NOT IN (42, 99, 230)
    GROUP BY meter_id
) AS t
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = t.meter_id
INNER JOIN meters.customers AS c ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id
WHERE m.utility = 'electricity'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY kwh DESC
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Day and night load profile
exercises.task: Tariffs charge more during the day (07:00–22:59 local time) than at night, so the team wants to know how differently each customer segment uses electricity. Using January 2026 electricity data (ts < '2026-02-01', UTC), return per segment the average 15-minute consumption in day hours and in night hours, and the day/night ratio. Remove duplicates first (keep the newest ingested_at). Interval consumption = value − the previous reading's value, even across a gap. A reading counts as day when the local hour (Europe/Sarajevo) of its ts is 7 to 22. Skip each meter's first reading, and leave out meters 42, 99 and 230.
exercises.cols: segment, day_avg_kwh, night_avg_kwh (both rounded to 3 decimals), day_night_ratio (rounded to 2 decimals, calculated from the unrounded averages)
exercises.hint: Build it in steps: dedup with GROUP BY meter_id, ts + argMax(value, ingested_at); then lagInFrame and row_number OVER (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts); then avgIf(kwh, local_hour BETWEEN 7 AND 22) and avgIf(kwh, NOT …) per segment.
exercises.solution:
WITH
    dedup AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, argMax(value, ingested_at) AS value
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id <= 200 AND meter_id NOT IN (42, 99, 230) AND ts < '2026-02-01'
        GROUP BY meter_id, ts
    ),
    deltas AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts,
               value - lagInFrame(value) OVER w AS kwh,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn
        FROM dedup
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts)
    ),
    profile AS
    (
        SELECT c.segment AS segment,
               avgIf(d.kwh, toHour(toTimeZone(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo')) BETWEEN 7 AND 22) AS day_avg,
               avgIf(d.kwh, NOT (toHour(toTimeZone(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo')) BETWEEN 7 AND 22)) AS night_avg
        FROM deltas AS d
        INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
        INNER JOIN meters.customers AS c ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id
        WHERE d.rn > 1
        GROUP BY c.segment
    )
SELECT segment,
       round(day_avg, 3) AS day_avg_kwh,
       round(night_avg, 3) AS night_avg_kwh,
       round(day_avg / night_avg, 2) AS day_night_ratio
FROM profile
ORDER BY segment

exercises.title: Find duplicates
exercises.task: Per utility, count the duplicate keys (a (meter_id, ts) with more than one row) and how many of them are conflicting (the copies have different values).
exercises.hint: GROUP BY meter_id, ts HAVING count() > 1, with uniqExact(value) to spot conflicts, then join to meters.
exercises.solution:
SELECT m.utility, count() AS duplicate_keys, countIf(d.distinct_values > 1) AS conflicting_keys
FROM
(
    SELECT meter_id, ts, uniqExact(value) AS distinct_values
    FROM meters.readings
    GROUP BY meter_id, ts
    HAVING count() > 1
) AS d
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
GROUP BY m.utility
ORDER BY m.utility

exercises.title: Missing intervals
exercises.task: Each electricity meter should have 8,640 distinct timestamps in Q1 (90 days × 96), and each water meter 2,160 (90 × 24). Return the 5 meters with the most missing timestamps.
exercises.hint: Count received timestamps with uniqExact(ts) so duplicates don't count twice.
exercises.solution:
SELECT r.meter_id, m.utility,
       if(m.utility = 'electricity', 8640, 2160) AS expected,
       uniqExact(r.ts) AS received,
       expected - received AS missing
FROM meters.readings AS r
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = r.meter_id
GROUP BY r.meter_id, m.utility
ORDER BY missing DESC, r.meter_id
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Counter going backwards
exercises.task: A cumulative register should never go down. After deduplicating (keep the newest ingested_at), list every reading whose value is lower than the meter's previous reading.
exercises.hint: Without deduplication you get false alarms from the conflicting copies. Skip each meter's first row (row_number() > 1).
exercises.solution:
WITH dedup AS
(
    SELECT meter_id, ts, argMax(value, ingested_at) AS value
    FROM meters.readings
    GROUP BY meter_id, ts
)
SELECT meter_id, ts, prev_value, value
FROM
(
    SELECT meter_id, ts, value,
           lagInFrame(value) OVER w AS prev_value,
           row_number() OVER w AS rn
    FROM dedup
    WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts)
)
WHERE rn > 1 AND value < prev_value
ORDER BY meter_id, ts

exercises.title: Spike detection
exercises.task: Find electricity spikes. After deduplicating, compute each interval's consumption rate in kWh per hour: (value − prev_value) / minutes since the previous reading × 60. Ignore negative deltas. A spike is a rate more than 20 times that meter's median rate. Dividing by the minutes stops a gap, such as a 3-day outage, from looking like a spike.
exercises.hint: Calculate the median per meter in a separate CTE and join it back. Convert to Float64 before dividing.
exercises.solution:
WITH
    dedup AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, argMax(value, ingested_at) AS value
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id <= 200
        GROUP BY meter_id, ts
    ),
    d AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts,
               value - lagInFrame(value) OVER w AS delta,
               dateDiff('minute', lagInFrame(ts) OVER w, ts) AS minutes,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn
        FROM dedup
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts)
    ),
    rates AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, delta, toFloat64(delta) / minutes * 60 AS rate
        FROM d
        WHERE rn > 1 AND delta >= 0
    ),
    med AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, quantileExact(0.5)(rate) AS median_rate
        FROM rates
        GROUP BY meter_id
    )
SELECT r.meter_id, r.ts, r.delta
FROM rates AS r
INNER JOIN med ON med.meter_id = r.meter_id
WHERE r.rate > 20 * med.median_rate
ORDER BY r.meter_id, r.ts

exercises.title: Late arrivals
exercises.task: Per UTC month, count all reading rows, the rows that arrived more than 1 day after their timestamp, and the late share as a percentage.
exercises.cols: month (first day of the month, e.g. 2026-01-01), readings, late, late_pct (rounded to 2 decimals)
exercises.hint: ingested_at > ts + INTERVAL 1 DAY
exercises.solution:
SELECT toStartOfMonth(ts) AS month,
       count() AS readings,
       countIf(ingested_at > ts + INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS late,
       round(late / readings * 100, 2) AS late_pct
FROM meters.readings
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month

exercises.title: Daylight-saving day
exercises.task: Readings are stored in UTC, but customers are billed by local days. For meter 6, count the distinct readings per local date (Europe/Sarajevo) for 2026-03-28, 03-29 and 03-30. On the 29th the clocks move forward, so that day has only 23 hours: 92 fifteen-minute readings instead of 96.
exercises.hint: toDate(ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo'), and uniqExact(ts) so duplicates don't count twice.
exercises.solution:
SELECT toDate(ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo') AS local_date, uniqExact(ts) AS readings
FROM meters.readings
WHERE meter_id = 6 AND local_date BETWEEN '2026-03-28' AND '2026-03-30'
GROUP BY local_date
ORDER BY local_date

exercises.title: Show the outage
exercises.task: Meter 17 had an outage. Count its distinct readings per UTC day from 2026-02-08 to 2026-02-14. Days without readings must still appear, with 0. Let ClickHouse fill them in; don't build a calendar table.
exercises.hint: ORDER BY day WITH FILL FROM toDate('2026-02-08') TO toDate('2026-02-15')
exercises.solution:
SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, uniqExact(ts) AS readings
FROM meters.readings
WHERE meter_id = 17 AND ts >= '2026-02-08' AND ts < '2026-02-15'
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY day WITH FILL FROM toDate('2026-02-08') TO toDate('2026-02-15')

exercises.title: 7-day rolling average
exercises.task: For meter 3, calculate daily UTC consumption with the method from exercise 17 (last value of the day minus last value of the previous day). Add a 7-day rolling average: the current day and the 6 days before it. Return 2026-03-25 to 2026-03-31.
exercises.cols: day, kwh, avg_7d (both rounded to 2 decimals)
exercises.hint: Calculate the window before you filter to Mar 25–31, or the first days will average fewer than 7 values. avg(kwh) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
exercises.solution:
WITH
    daily AS
    (
        SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, argMax(value, (ts, ingested_at)) AS day_end
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id = 3 AND ts >= '2026-03-17'
        GROUP BY day
    ),
    cons AS
    (
        SELECT day, day_end - lagInFrame(day_end) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS kwh
        FROM daily
    )
SELECT day, round(kwh, 2) AS kwh, round(avg_7d, 2) AS avg_7d
FROM
(
    SELECT day, kwh, avg(kwh) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_7d
    FROM cons
    WHERE day >= '2026-03-18'
)
WHERE day >= '2026-03-25'
ORDER BY day

exercises.title: Month-over-month change
exercises.task: Using the max − min method per meter and UTC month (electricity only, leaving out meters 42, 99 and 230), sum consumption per segment and month, then add the percentage change from the previous month. January has no previous month, so its change must be NULL, not 0 or infinity.
exercises.cols: segment, month (first day of the month, e.g. 2026-01-01), kwh, mom_pct (both rounded to 2 decimals)
exercises.hint: lagInFrame(toNullable(kwh)) OVER (PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY month) returns NULL on the first row. Convert to Float64 before dividing: Decimal division keeps only the input scale (3 decimals), so it would give −9.3 instead of −9.36.
exercises.solution:
WITH monthly AS
(
    SELECT c.segment, t.month, toFloat64(sum(t.kwh)) AS kwh
    FROM
    (
        SELECT meter_id, toStartOfMonth(ts) AS month, max(value) - min(value) AS kwh
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id <= 200 AND meter_id NOT IN (42, 99, 230)
        GROUP BY meter_id, month
    ) AS t
    INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = t.meter_id
    INNER JOIN meters.customers AS c ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.segment, t.month
)
SELECT segment, month, round(kwh, 2) AS kwh,
       round((kwh - prev) / prev * 100, 2) AS mom_pct
FROM
(
    SELECT segment, month, kwh,
           lagInFrame(toNullable(kwh)) OVER (PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY month) AS prev
    FROM monthly
)
ORDER BY segment, month

exercises.title: Peak demand
exercises.task: Peak demand in kW is the highest 15-minute consumption × 4. For January 2026 electricity (ts < '2026-02-01', UTC; deduplicated; leaving out meters 42, 99 and 230), use only intervals whose previous reading is exactly 15 minutes earlier. Return the 5 meters with the highest peak and when the peak happened. If a meter reaches its peak more than once, report the latest time.
exercises.hint: dateDiff('minute', lagInFrame(ts) OVER w, ts) = 15 removes intervals that span a gap. argMax(ts, (kwh, ts)) breaks ties by picking the latest ts.
exercises.solution:
WITH
    dedup AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, argMax(value, ingested_at) AS value
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id <= 200 AND meter_id NOT IN (42, 99, 230) AND ts < '2026-02-01'
        GROUP BY meter_id, ts
    ),
    d AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts,
               value - lagInFrame(value) OVER w AS kwh,
               dateDiff('minute', lagInFrame(ts) OVER w, ts) AS minutes,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn
        FROM dedup
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts)
    )
SELECT meter_id, round(max(kwh * 4), 2) AS peak_kw, argMax(ts, (kwh, ts)) AS peak_ts
FROM d
WHERE rn > 1 AND minutes = 15
GROUP BY meter_id
ORDER BY peak_kw DESC
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Materialized view
exercises.task: Build a pre-aggregation that updates itself on every insert. Create practice.raw_readings with the same structure as meters.readings. Create practice.daily_agg (AggregatingMergeTree) holding, per meter and UTC day, the reading count, min(value) and max(value). Connect them with a materialized view. Then insert meters 1–20 in two batches: January first, then February–March. Run the check query and paste its result.

The MV uses countState(), minState(value), maxState(value), and you read them with countMerge, minMerge, maxMerge. Create the MV before you insert. For simple functions like min, max and sum, SimpleAggregateFunction(min, …) is a lighter alternative you will often see in real projects; try it after you get this version working.

FROM practice.daily_agg
WHERE meter_id = 1 AND day BETWEEN '2026-01-31' AND '2026-02-02'
GROUP BY day

exercises.solution:
CREATE TABLE practice.raw_readings AS meters.readings;
CREATE TABLE practice.daily_agg
(
    meter_id  UInt32,
    day       Date,
    readings  AggregateFunction(count),
    min_value AggregateFunction(min, Decimal(12, 3)),
    max_value AggregateFunction(max, Decimal(12, 3))
)
ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree
ORDER BY (meter_id, day);
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW practice.daily_agg_mv TO practice.daily_agg AS
SELECT meter_id, toDate(ts) AS day, countState() AS readings, minState(value) AS min_value, maxState(value) AS max_value
FROM practice.raw_readings
GROUP BY meter_id, day;
INSERT INTO practice.raw_readings SELECT * FROM meters.readings WHERE meter_id <= 20 AND ts < '2026-02-01';
INSERT INTO practice.raw_readings SELECT * FROM meters.readings WHERE meter_id <= 20 AND ts >= '2026-02-01';

-- check query
SELECT day, countMerge(readings) AS readings, maxMerge(max_value) - minMerge(min_value) AS spread
FROM practice.daily_agg
WHERE meter_id = 1 AND day BETWEEN '2026-01-31' AND '2026-02-02'

exercises.task: Dictionaries are in-memory lookups and are often faster than JOINs. (1) Create a user dict_reader with password dict_reader_pw that can connect only from inside the server (HOST LOCAL), and give it SELECT on meters.*. (2) Create a dictionary practice.meter_info keyed by meter_id, with the attributes utility, segment and city, built from a query that joins meters and customers, using that user. Run the check query and paste its result.

FROM meters.readings
WHERE dictGet('practice.meter_info', 'utility', toUInt64(meter_id)) = 'electricity' AND ts < '2026-02-01'

DROP USER IF EXISTS dict_reader;
CREATE USER dict_reader IDENTIFIED BY 'dict_reader_pw' HOST LOCAL;
GRANT SELECT ON meters.* TO dict_reader;
CREATE DICTIONARY practice.meter_info
(
    meter_id UInt64,
    utility  String,
    segment  String,
    city     String
)
PRIMARY KEY meter_id
SOURCE(CLICKHOUSE(QUERY 'SELECT m.meter_id, m.utility, c.segment, c.city FROM meters.meters AS m INNER JOIN meters.customers AS c ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id' USER 'dict_reader' PASSWORD 'dict_reader_pw'))

WHERE dictGet('practice.meter_info', 'utility', toUInt64(meter_id)) = 'electricity' AND ts < '2026-02-01'

exercises.title: Sensor time series
exercises.task: Run this one in the browser playground. Sensor readings work much like meter readings. For sensor_id = 182 from 2022-06-01 to 2022-06-07 (filter on timestamp; the date column is empty), return per day: readings, min, avg and max temperature, and the largest gap between two consecutive readings, where gap = dateDiff('minute', previous timestamp, timestamp). Count every reading in the stats; only the week's very first reading has no gap.
exercises.cols: day, readings, min_temp, avg_temp, max_temp (temps rounded to 1 decimal), max_gap_min
exercises.hint: Calculate the gap with lagInFrame(timestamp) over the whole week, then aggregate per day. Don't filter out the first row, or June 1 loses a reading: use max(if(rn > 1, gap_min, NULL)) so only the gap ignores it. dateDiff('minute', …) counts minute boundaries crossed, which can be 1 more than seconds / 60.
exercises.solution:
SELECT toDate(timestamp) AS day,
       count() AS readings,
       round(min(temperature), 1) AS min_temp,
       round(avg(temperature), 1) AS avg_temp,
       round(max(temperature), 1) AS max_temp,
       max(if(rn > 1, gap_min, NULL)) AS max_gap_min
FROM
(
    SELECT timestamp, temperature,
           dateDiff('minute', lagInFrame(timestamp) OVER w, timestamp) AS gap_min,
           row_number() OVER w AS rn
    FROM environmental.sensors
    WHERE sensor_id = 182 AND timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-06-08 00:00:00'
    WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY timestamp)
)
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY day

exercises.title: February bills
exercises.task: Calculate February 2026 bills for customers 17, 42, 50, 77 and 99. February means the reading's local month (Europe/Sarajevo). Use the clean-consumption rules from the Meter data rules section: (1) deduplicate, keeping the newest ingested_at; (2) drop a glitch reading whose value is higher than the next reading, unless the next reading is a meter replacement; (3) interval consumption = value − previous value, except that the first reading at or after a replacement counts its own value; (4) skip each meter's very first reading. A replacement happens at install_date 00:00 UTC, i.e. toDateTime(install_date, 'UTC'); readings with ts at or after that come from the new meter. Each interval's consumption belongs to the date and hour of its reading's ts (the end of the interval). Electricity uses the day rate when the reading's local hour is between 7 and 22 (7 ≤ hour < 23) and the night rate otherwise; water uses its flat rate. Prices come from meters.tariffs by utility and segment.
exercises.cols: customer_id, electricity_kwh, water_m3, total_eur (all rounded to 2 decimals)
exercises.hint: Work out rate_type (day / night / flat) on each consumption row, then do an equality JOIN to tariffs on (utility, segment, rate_type). Calculate the deltas over the whole quarter and filter to February at the end, so February 1 gets its delta from January 31.
exercises.solution:
WITH
    dedup AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, argMax(value, ingested_at) AS value
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id IN (SELECT meter_id FROM meters.meters WHERE customer_id IN (17, 42, 50, 77, 99))
        GROUP BY meter_id, ts
    ),
    flagged AS
    (
        SELECT d.meter_id, d.ts, d.value,
               leadInFrame(d.value) OVER w AS next_value,
               leadInFrame(d.ts) OVER w AS next_ts,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn,
               count() OVER w AS cnt
        FROM dedup AS d
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY d.meter_id ORDER BY d.ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
    ),
    clean AS
    (
        SELECT f.meter_id, f.ts, f.value
        FROM flagged AS f
        INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = f.meter_id
        WHERE NOT (f.rn < f.cnt AND f.value > f.next_value
                   AND NOT (f.ts < toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC') AND f.next_ts >= toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC')))
    ),
    deltas AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, value,
               lagInFrame(value) OVER w AS prev_value,
               lagInFrame(ts) OVER w AS prev_ts,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn
        FROM clean
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts)
    ),
    consumption AS
    (
        SELECT d.meter_id, d.ts, m.utility, m.customer_id,
               if(d.prev_ts < toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC') AND d.ts >= toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC'),
                  d.value, d.value - d.prev_value) AS amount,
               toHour(toTimeZone(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo')) AS local_hour,
               multiIf(m.utility = 'water', 'flat', local_hour >= 7 AND local_hour < 23, 'day', 'night') AS rate_type
        FROM deltas AS d
        INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
        WHERE d.rn > 1
          AND toStartOfMonth(toTimeZone(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo')) = '2026-02-01'
    )
SELECT x.customer_id AS customer_id,
       round(sumIf(x.amount, x.utility = 'electricity'), 2) AS electricity_kwh,
       round(sumIf(x.amount, x.utility = 'water'), 2) AS water_m3,
       round(sum(x.amount * t.price_eur), 2) AS total_eur
FROM consumption AS x
INNER JOIN meters.customers AS c ON c.customer_id = x.customer_id
INNER JOIN meters.tariffs AS t ON t.utility = x.utility AND t.segment = c.segment AND t.rate_type = x.rate_type
GROUP BY x.customer_id
ORDER BY x.customer_id

exercises.title: March completeness report
exercises.task: Data quality KPI for March 2026 (UTC). Per utility, return: meters, expected readings (31 × 96 per electricity meter, 31 × 24 per water meter), received distinct readings, completeness % and the number of meters below 99% complete.
exercises.cols: utility, meters, expected_readings, received_readings, completeness_pct (rounded to 2 decimals), meters_below_99
exercises.hint: Count distinct (meter_id, ts) per meter first, work out each meter's expected count, then aggregate per utility.
exercises.solution:
SELECT m.utility,
       count() AS meters,
       sum(p.expected) AS expected_readings,
       sum(p.received) AS received_readings,
       round(received_readings / expected_readings * 100, 2) AS completeness_pct,
       countIf(p.received / p.expected < 0.99) AS meters_below_99
FROM
(
    SELECT r.meter_id, uniqExact(r.ts) AS received, if(any(m2.utility) = 'electricity', 31 * 96, 31 * 24) AS expected
    FROM meters.readings AS r
    INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m2 ON m2.meter_id = r.meter_id
    WHERE r.ts >= '2026-03-01' AND r.ts < '2026-04-01'
    GROUP BY r.meter_id
) AS p
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = p.meter_id
GROUP BY m.utility
ORDER BY m.utility

exercises.title: Water leak detection
exercises.task: A household or office should use no water in the middle of the night. For residential and commercial water meters (deduplicated, skipping the first reading), a night has continuous flow when every reading with local hour 2, 3 or 4 has consumption > 0. Find runs of at least 7 consecutive nights like that.
exercises.hint: This is the "gaps and islands" pattern. Number each meter's flagged nights with row_number(); night minus that number is the same for every night in an unbroken run, so you can group by it. subtractDays(night, rn) works on Date.
exercises.solution:
WITH
    dedup AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, argMax(value, ingested_at) AS value
        FROM meters.readings
        WHERE meter_id > 200
        GROUP BY meter_id, ts
    ),
    d AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts,
               value - lagInFrame(value) OVER w AS m3,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn
        FROM dedup
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts)
    ),
    nights AS
    (
        SELECT d.meter_id AS meter_id, toDate(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo') AS night
        FROM d
        INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
        INNER JOIN meters.customers AS c ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id
        WHERE d.rn > 1
          AND c.segment IN ('residential', 'commercial')
          AND toHour(toTimeZone(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo')) BETWEEN 2 AND 4
        GROUP BY d.meter_id, night
        HAVING min(d.m3) > 0
    ),
    islands AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, night,
               subtractDays(night, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY night)) AS grp
        FROM nights
    )
SELECT meter_id, min(night) AS leak_start, count() AS nights
FROM islands
GROUP BY meter_id, grp
HAVING nights >= 7
ORDER BY meter_id

exercises.title: Daily consumption table
exercises.task: Build the table your reports would read from. Create practice.daily_consumption (meter_id UInt32, local_date Date, consumption Decimal(18, 3)) ordered by (meter_id, local_date) and fill it for all meters and the whole quarter. Use the clean-consumption rules from the Meter data rules section: (1) deduplicate, keeping the newest ingested_at; (2) drop a glitch reading whose value is higher than the next reading, unless the next reading is a meter replacement; (3) interval consumption = value − previous value, except that the first reading at or after a replacement counts its own value; (4) skip each meter's very first reading. A replacement happens at install_date 00:00 UTC, i.e. toDateTime(install_date, 'UTC'); readings with ts at or after that come from the new meter. Each interval's consumption belongs to the date and hour of its reading's ts (the end of the interval). Each interval's consumption counts toward the local date (Europe/Sarajevo) of its reading's ts. Run the check query and paste its result.
exercises.hint: Reuse your exercise 36 CTEs without the customer filter and pricing, then GROUP BY meter_id, local_date in the INSERT … SELECT.
exercises.verify:
SELECT m.utility, count() AS rows, round(sum(d.consumption), 2) AS total
FROM practice.daily_consumption AS d
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
GROUP BY m.utility
ORDER BY m.utility
exercises.solution:
CREATE TABLE practice.daily_consumption
(
    meter_id    UInt32,
    local_date  Date,
    consumption Decimal(18, 3)
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
ORDER BY (meter_id, local_date);
INSERT INTO practice.daily_consumption
WITH
    dedup AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, argMax(value, ingested_at) AS value
        FROM meters.readings
        GROUP BY meter_id, ts
    ),
    flagged AS
    (
        SELECT d.meter_id, d.ts, d.value,
               leadInFrame(d.value) OVER w AS next_value,
               leadInFrame(d.ts) OVER w AS next_ts,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn,
               count() OVER w AS cnt
        FROM dedup AS d
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY d.meter_id ORDER BY d.ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
    ),
    clean AS
    (
        SELECT f.meter_id, f.ts, f.value
        FROM flagged AS f
        INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = f.meter_id
        WHERE NOT (f.rn < f.cnt AND f.value > f.next_value
                   AND NOT (f.ts < toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC') AND f.next_ts >= toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC')))
    ),
    deltas AS
    (
        SELECT meter_id, ts, value,
               lagInFrame(value) OVER w AS prev_value,
               lagInFrame(ts) OVER w AS prev_ts,
               row_number() OVER w AS rn
        FROM clean
        WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY meter_id ORDER BY ts)
    )
SELECT d.meter_id,
       toDate(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo') AS local_date,
       sum(if(d.prev_ts < toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC') AND d.ts >= toDateTime(m.install_date, 'UTC'),
              d.value, d.value - d.prev_value)) AS consumption
FROM deltas AS d
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
WHERE d.rn > 1
GROUP BY d.meter_id, local_date;

-- check query
SELECT m.utility, count() AS rows, round(sum(d.consumption), 2) AS total
FROM practice.daily_consumption AS d
INNER JOIN meters.meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
GROUP BY m.utility
ORDER BY m.utility

exercises.title: Design the production schema
exercises.task: Design the ClickHouse schema you would propose for the real project: about 500,000 electricity and water meters, 15-minute readings, a feed that sends duplicates, corrections and late data, and reports by customer, local day and month. Write the DDL in your SQL notes: a raw table, the deduplication strategy, a materialized view or pre-aggregation for hourly or daily data, TTL or retention, and ORDER BY / PARTITION BY choices. Add short comments explaining why. Claude reviews it like a senior engineer would.
exercises.hint: Think about which queries run most often (one meter over time? all meters for one day?), how many rows a year that is (500k × 96 × 365 ≈ 17.5B), and what happens when a correction arrives for a day that is already aggregated.
exercises.solution:
-- One reasonable design (there are others):
-- 1. Raw landing table, append-only, keeps every version. Cheap to re-process.
CREATE TABLE energy.readings_raw
(
    meter_id    UInt32,
    ts          DateTime('UTC') CODEC(DoubleDelta, ZSTD),
    value       Decimal(14, 3)  CODEC(Delta, ZSTD),        -- cumulative counter: small deltas compress very well
    ingested_at DateTime('UTC') CODEC(DoubleDelta, ZSTD),
    source      LowCardinality(String)
)
ENGINE = MergeTree                              -- plain MergeTree: keeps every delivered version (audit, replay)
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts)                       -- monthly partitions: ~1.5B rows each, easy DROP/reload
ORDER BY (meter_id, ts, ingested_at)            -- most queries: one meter / many meters over a time range
TTL ingested_at + INTERVAL 1 YEAR DELETE;       -- raw retention; the clean layer is kept longer
-- 1b. Clean layer: one row per (meter_id, ts), newest version wins. Filled from raw by an MV or the dbt job.
CREATE TABLE energy.readings
(
    meter_id    UInt32,
    ts          DateTime('UTC') CODEC(DoubleDelta, ZSTD),
    value       Decimal(14, 3)  CODEC(Delta, ZSTD),
    ingested_at DateTime('UTC') CODEC(DoubleDelta, ZSTD)
)
ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(ingested_at)        -- dedup on merge; read with FINAL (or argMax) for exact results
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts)
ORDER BY (meter_id, ts);
-- 2. Hourly aggregate fed by MV. Cumulative registers need deltas, which need the previous reading,
--    so a common approach is to store min/max per hour (Aggregating) and compute consumption as
--    differences between consecutive hours at query time, OR run a scheduled (e.g. hourly) INSERT…SELECT
--    job that recomputes recent days from readings_raw FINAL, so late data and corrections are absorbed.
-- 3. daily_consumption (ReplacingMergeTree(version) ORDER BY (meter_id, local_date)) rebuilt per day by the job;
--    reports by customer join via a dictionary (meter -> customer, segment, tariff), not a big JOIN.

exercises.title: Sensor fleet in one day
exercises.task: Get a first picture of a big fleet. For 2022-06-01 (UTC), return the 5 sensor types with the most readings, with the number of distinct sensors of each type. The table is sorted by (timestamp, sensor_id), so always filter on timestamp first; the date column is empty.
exercises.hint: timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-06-02 00:00:00'. Use a half-open range like this for every time filter, so midnight is never counted twice.
exercises.solution:
SELECT sensor_type, uniqExact(sensor_id) AS sensors, count() AS readings
FROM environmental.sensors
WHERE timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-06-02 00:00:00'
GROUP BY sensor_type
ORDER BY readings DESC
LIMIT 5

exercises.title: Gaps across 5,000 sensors
exercises.task: Find the largest gap between two consecutive readings of each BME280 sensor on 2022-06-01, counting only sensors with at least 100 readings that day. Return how many sensors qualify and how many of them had a gap longer than 30 minutes. This is the same completeness check you would run on every meter every night. The table is sorted by (timestamp, sensor_id), so always filter on timestamp first; the date column is empty.
exercises.hint: Window functions work, but arrays are often faster in ClickHouse: arraySort(groupArray(toUInt32(timestamp))), then arrayDifference, then arrayMax, all per sensor_id. A gap longer than 30 minutes means more than 1,800 seconds.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count() AS sensors, countIf(max_gap_s > 1800) AS sensors_with_gap_over_30min
FROM
(
    SELECT sensor_id,
           arrayMax(arrayDifference(arraySort(groupArray(toUInt32(timestamp))))) AS max_gap_s
    FROM environmental.sensors
    WHERE sensor_type = 'BME280'
      AND timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-06-02 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY sensor_id
    HAVING count() >= 100
)

exercises.title: Stuck sensors
exercises.task: A healthy sensor's temperature changes over a day. A sensor reporting the same value all day is stuck, just like a meter register that never moves. For BME280 sensors on 2022-06-01 with at least 100 readings, find the ones whose temperature never changed. Return how many are stuck, and how many of those are stuck below −40 °C, which is a hardware error value rather than a real temperature. The table is sorted by (timestamp, sensor_id), so always filter on timestamp first; the date column is empty.
exercises.hint: Per sensor: HAVING count() >= 100 AND min(temperature) = max(temperature). Keep any(temperature) AS stuck_value, then count in an outer query.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count() AS stuck_sensors, countIf(stuck_value < -40) AS stuck_at_error_value
FROM
(
    SELECT sensor_id, any(temperature) AS stuck_value
    FROM environmental.sensors
    WHERE sensor_type = 'BME280'
      AND timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-06-02 00:00:00'
    GROUP BY sensor_id
    HAVING count() >= 100 AND min(temperature) = max(temperature)
)

exercises.title: Hourly fleet heartbeat
exercises.task: For DHT22 sensors on 2022-06-01, return per hour the number of readings and the number of distinct sensors that reported. A dip in a chart of this result is how you would spot a feed outage. The table is sorted by (timestamp, sensor_id), so always filter on timestamp first; the date column is empty.

FROM environmental.sensors
WHERE sensor_type = 'DHT22'
  AND timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-06-02 00:00:00'

exercises.title: The silent wrong answer
exercises.task: (1) Count the readings of sensor_id = 182 in June 2022 and return them with the first and last timestamp. That is the result to paste. (2) Then run SELECT count() FROM environmental.sensors WHERE sensor_id = 182 with no time filter, two or three times. Compare the numbers and the rows read shown under the result. In Your SQL, write in two sentences what happened and why. The playground stops reading after 1 billion rows and returns what it has, without an error.
exercises.hint: The table is sorted by (timestamp, sensor_id). A filter on sensor_id alone can't skip any data, because sensor 182 appears in every time range. Your server has a similar setting: read_overflow_mode = 'break' returns partial results.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count() AS readings, min(timestamp) AS first_ts, max(timestamp) AS last_ts
FROM environmental.sensors
WHERE sensor_id = 182
  AND timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-07-01 00:00:00';

-- Without a time filter the count changes between runs (e.g. 280,089 then 91,743):
-- sensor_id is the SECOND column of ORDER BY (timestamp, sensor_id), so the index cannot skip anything,
-- ClickHouse reads ~1B of the 20.7B rows, hits max_rows_to_read with read_overflow_mode = 'break',
-- and returns a partial count with no error. Always put the leading sort-key column in the WHERE.

exercises.title: Physically impossible values
exercises.task: Validate before you aggregate. For the temperature sensor types (BME280, BMP180, BMP280, DHT22, DS18B20, HTU21D) on 2022-06-01, count all readings, the invalid ones (temperature below −40 or above 60), and the invalid share in %. In the meter project you'll run the same check for negative or impossible consumption. The table is sorted by (timestamp, sensor_id), so always filter on timestamp first; the date column is empty.
exercises.cols: sensor_type, readings, invalid, invalid_pct (rounded to 2 decimals)
exercises.hint: sensor_type is an Enum, so you can compare it with strings: sensor_type IN ('BME280', …).
exercises.solution:
SELECT sensor_type,
       count() AS readings,
       countIf(temperature < -40 OR temperature > 60) AS invalid,
       round(invalid / readings * 100, 2) AS invalid_pct
FROM environmental.sensors
WHERE timestamp >= '2022-06-01 00:00:00' AND timestamp < '2022-06-02 00:00:00'
  AND sensor_type IN ('BME280', 'BMP180', 'BMP280', 'DHT22', 'DS18B20', 'HTU21D')
GROUP BY sensor_type
ORDER BY toString(sensor_type)

exercises.title: Filter on the sort key
exercises.task: The GitHub events table is sorted by (repo_id, event_type, created_at). For the ClickHouse repository (repo_id = '60246359', a string), return the 5 most common event types in 2023 and the number of distinct people (actor_login) behind each. Then run the same query filtering on repo_name = 'ClickHouse/ClickHouse' instead, and write in Your SQL how many rows each version read.
exercises.hint: The web UI shows rows read under the result. Expect hundreds of thousands of rows for one filter and hundreds of millions for the other.
exercises.solution:
SELECT event_type, count() AS events, uniqExact(actor_login) AS people
FROM github.github_events
WHERE repo_id = '60246359'
  AND created_at >= '2023-01-01 00:00:00' AND created_at < '2024-01-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY event_type
ORDER BY events DESC
LIMIT 5;
-- repo_id filter: a few hundred thousand rows read. repo_name filter: ~250M rows read for the same answer,
-- because repo_name is not in the ORDER BY key. Meter tables: put meter_id first for the same reason.

exercises.title: Enums on the full UK table
exercises.task: In the playground's copy of the UK table, type is an Enum with readable labels (detached, flat …); in your local copy it is a plain number. For sales dated in 2022, return per property type the number of sales and the average price. Afterwards, compare with your local table and work out which number stands for which label.
exercises.cols: type, sales, avg_price (rounded to whole pounds)
exercises.hint: date >= '2022-01-01' AND date < '2023-01-01'. Run SELECT DISTINCT type FROM uk.uk_price_paid to see the Enum labels.

exercises.title: What's in the bucket
exercises.task: The meter head-end system delivers one Parquet file per day into the bucket, under readings/YYYY/MM/DD.parquet. Without loading anything, query the files in place and return the number of files, the total rows, and the first and last file path. The bucket is reached through the named collection lake, which holds the URL and the keys so they never appear in your SQL: s3(lake, filename = 'readings/…').
exercises.cols: files, rows, first_file, last_file (the full _path, including the bucket name)
exercises.hint: filename = 'readings/**.parquet' matches every folder level. The virtual column _path holds the file each row came from. Group by it in a subquery, then summarise.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count() AS files, sum(rows) AS rows, min(file) AS first_file, max(file) AS last_file
FROM
(
    SELECT _path AS file, count() AS rows
    FROM s3(lake, filename = 'readings/**.parquet')
    GROUP BY file
)

exercises.title: Delivery day is not reading day
exercises.task: Files are named after the day they were delivered, not the day the readings were measured. Query only the March 2026 files and return how many files there are, how many rows they hold, and how many of those rows were measured before 2026-03-01 00:00 UTC. Look at the file list: one of them shouldn't be there. The bucket is reached through the named collection lake, which holds the URL and the keys so they never appear in your SQL: s3(lake, filename = 'readings/…').
exercises.hint: filename = 'readings/2026/03/*.parquet'. uniqExact(_path) counts the files.
exercises.solution:
SELECT uniqExact(_path) AS files, count() AS rows, countIf(ts < '2026-03-01') AS readings_before_march
FROM s3(lake, filename = 'readings/2026/03/*.parquet')

exercises.title: Load January into a raw table
exercises.task: Create database lake and table lake.readings_raw with the four reading columns plus source_file LowCardinality(String) (which file the row came from) and loaded_at DateTime('UTC') DEFAULT now(). Use a MergeTree partitioned by month and ordered by (meter_id, ts). Load only the files delivered in January 2026. Keep every row as delivered, without deduplicating: raw tables are a faithful copy of the source. Run the check query and paste its result.
exercises.hint: Parquet columns come back Nullable. ClickHouse converts them to your non-Nullable columns on INSERT as long as no value is NULL. Fill source_file from _path.
exercises.verify:
SELECT count() AS rows, uniqExact(source_file) AS files, min(ts) AS first_ts, max(ts) AS last_ts
FROM lake.readings_raw
exercises.solution:
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS lake;
CREATE DATABASE lake;
CREATE TABLE lake.readings_raw
(
    meter_id    UInt32,
    ts          DateTime('UTC'),
    value       Decimal(12, 3),
    ingested_at DateTime('UTC'),
    source_file LowCardinality(String),
    loaded_at   DateTime('UTC') DEFAULT now()
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(ts)
ORDER BY (meter_id, ts);
INSERT INTO lake.readings_raw (meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at, source_file)
SELECT meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at, _path
FROM s3(lake, filename = 'readings/2026/01/*.parquet');

-- check query
SELECT count() AS rows, uniqExact(source_file) AS files, min(ts) AS first_ts, max(ts) AS last_ts
FROM lake.readings_raw

exercises.title: Load only new files
exercises.task: A nightly Airflow job runs the same load every day, so it must pick up only files it hasn't loaded yet, and running it twice must change nothing. Write one INSERT that loads every file not yet in lake.readings_raw. Run it, then run it again. Run the check query and paste its result.
exercises.hint: WHERE _path NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT source_file FROM lake.readings_raw). A filter on _path also lets ClickHouse skip reading those files at all. In production the S3Queue engine does this bookkeeping for you.
exercises.verify:
SELECT count() AS rows, uniqExact(source_file) AS files
FROM lake.readings_raw
exercises.solution:
INSERT INTO lake.readings_raw (meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at, source_file)
SELECT meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at, _path
FROM s3(lake, filename = 'readings/**.parquet')
WHERE _path NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT source_file FROM lake.readings_raw);
INSERT INTO lake.readings_raw (meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at, source_file)
SELECT meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at, _path
FROM s3(lake, filename = 'readings/**.parquet')
WHERE _path NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT source_file FROM lake.readings_raw);

-- check query
SELECT count() AS rows, uniqExact(source_file) AS files
FROM lake.readings_raw

exercises.title: Spot the resent file
exercises.task: Sometimes a supplier sends the same file twice under a different name. Using only lake.readings_raw, find files whose content is identical to another file: same row count and the same order-independent fingerprint of their rows. Return each duplicate with the file it copies, where file is the name that sorts later.
exercises.hint: Per source_file: count() and sum(cityHash64(meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at)). A sum of row hashes doesn't depend on row order. Join that result to itself on the fingerprint, with f.source_file > g.source_file.
exercises.solution:
WITH fp AS
(
    SELECT source_file, count() AS c, sum(cityHash64(meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at)) AS h
    FROM lake.readings_raw
    GROUP BY source_file
)
SELECT f.source_file AS file, g.source_file AS duplicate_of
FROM fp AS f
INNER JOIN fp AS g ON f.h = g.h AND f.c = g.c AND f.source_file > g.source_file
ORDER BY file

exercises.title: Your first dbt model
exercises.task: Run dbt from the repo folder with docker compose run --rm dbt …; your models live in dbt/meter_project/. Create models/staging/stg_readings.sql: one row per (meter_id, ts) from source('lake', 'readings_raw'), keeping the value with the newest ingested_at. Override the folder default (view) so it is saved as a MergeTree table ordered by (meter_id, ts) and partitioned by month. Run docker compose run --rm dbt run --select stg_readings, then run the check query and paste its result. If your answer to exercise 15 was right, the numbers will look familiar.
exercises.hint: {{ config(materialized='table', engine='MergeTree', order_by='(meter_id, ts)', partition_by='toYYYYMM(ts)') }}. Watch out: if you name the result max(ingested_at) AS ingested_at, the argMax next to it refers to that alias. Alias the source table and write r.ingested_at.
exercises.verify:
SELECT count() AS rows, sum(value) AS total_value
FROM analytics.stg_readings
exercises.solution:
-- ===== file: dbt/meter_project/models/staging/stg_readings.sql =====
{{ config(
    materialized = 'table',
    engine       = 'MergeTree',
    order_by     = '(meter_id, ts)',
    partition_by = 'toYYYYMM(ts)'
) }}

-- one row per (meter_id, ts): the newest delivery wins
-- note r.ingested_at: without the table alias, ClickHouse would resolve `ingested_at`
-- to the max(...) alias below and fail with "aggregate inside another aggregate"
select
    r.meter_id                     as meter_id,
    r.ts                           as ts,
    argMax(r.value, r.ingested_at) as value,
    max(r.ingested_at)             as ingested_at
from {{ source('lake', 'readings_raw') }} as r
group by r.meter_id, r.ts

-- ===== then run =====
-- docker compose run --rm dbt run --select stg_readings

-- ===== check query =====
SELECT count() AS rows, sum(value) AS total_value
FROM analytics.stg_readings

exercises.title: Chain models with ref()
exercises.task: Turn your exercise 39 query into models/marts/daily_consumption.sql, reading from {{ ref('stg_readings') }} and {{ ref('stg_meters') }} instead of the meters tables, and saved as a table ordered by (meter_id, local_date). Run docker compose run --rm dbt build: dbt works out the order from your ref() calls. Run the check query and paste its result. It should match exercise 39 exactly, because the data went through S3 and dbt but the logic is the same.
exercises.hint: stg_meters already has install_date per meter. After the run, open dbt/meter_project/target/compiled/… to see the plain ClickHouse SQL dbt sent.
exercises.verify:
SELECT m.utility, count() AS rows, round(sum(d.consumption), 2) AS total
FROM analytics.daily_consumption AS d
INNER JOIN analytics.stg_meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
GROUP BY m.utility
ORDER BY m.utility
exercises.solution:
-- ===== file: dbt/meter_project/models/marts/daily_consumption.sql =====
{{ config(
    materialized = 'table',
    engine       = 'MergeTree',
    order_by     = '(meter_id, local_date)'
) }}

with
    meters as (
        select meter_id, toDateTime(install_date, 'UTC') as installed_at
        from {{ ref('stg_meters') }}
    ),
    flagged as (
        select
            r.meter_id, r.ts, r.value,
            leadInFrame(r.value) over w as next_value,
            leadInFrame(r.ts)    over w as next_ts,
            row_number()         over w as rn,
            count()              over w as cnt
        from {{ ref('stg_readings') }} as r
        window w as (partition by r.meter_id order by r.ts rows between unbounded preceding and unbounded following)
    ),
    clean as (   -- drop glitches: higher than the next reading, unless the next one is a replacement
        select f.meter_id, f.ts, f.value
        from flagged as f
        inner join meters as m on m.meter_id = f.meter_id
        where not (f.rn < f.cnt and f.value > f.next_value
                   and not (f.ts < m.installed_at and f.next_ts >= m.installed_at))
    ),
    deltas as (
        select
            meter_id, ts, value,
            lagInFrame(value) over w as prev_value,
            lagInFrame(ts)    over w as prev_ts,
            row_number()      over w as rn
        from clean
        window w as (partition by meter_id order by ts)
    )
select
    d.meter_id                           as meter_id,
    toDate(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo')      as local_date,
    sum(if(d.prev_ts < m.installed_at and d.ts >= m.installed_at,
           d.value,                      -- first reading of a new meter counts from 0
           d.value - d.prev_value))      as consumption
from deltas as d
inner join meters as m on m.meter_id = d.meter_id
where d.rn > 1
group by d.meter_id, local_date

-- ===== then run =====
-- docker compose run --rm dbt build

-- ===== check query =====
SELECT m.utility, count() AS rows, round(sum(d.consumption), 2) AS total
FROM analytics.daily_consumption AS d
INNER JOIN analytics.stg_meters AS m ON m.meter_id = d.meter_id
GROUP BY m.utility
ORDER BY m.utility

exercises.title: Data tests
exercises.task: Add tests that run on every dbt build. (1) In models/marts/schema.yml: not_null on meter_id, local_date and consumption, plus a relationships test saying every meter_id exists in stg_meters. (2) Two singular tests in tests/: no negative consumption, and only one row per (meter_id, local_date). Run docker compose run --rm dbt test. Then break a test on purpose, for example by removing the replacement rule from step 3 of your model; rebuild and watch it fail. Paste both test outputs into Your result. Claude reviews this one.
exercises.hint: A singular test is a SELECT that returns the bad rows: zero rows means pass. In dbt 1.11, arguments for generic tests go under an arguments: key.
exercises.solution:
-- ===== file: dbt/meter_project/models/marts/schema.yml =====
version: 2
models:
  - name: daily_consumption
    description: Clean consumption per meter and local day (Europe/Sarajevo).
    columns:
      - name: meter_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              arguments:
                to: ref('stg_meters')
                field: meter_id
      - name: local_date
        data_tests: [not_null]
      - name: consumption
        data_tests: [not_null]

-- ===== file: dbt/meter_project/tests/assert_no_negative_consumption.sql =====
-- A singular test: dbt fails the test if this query returns any rows.
select meter_id, local_date, consumption
from {{ ref('daily_consumption') }}
where consumption < 0

-- ===== file: dbt/meter_project/tests/assert_one_row_per_meter_day.sql =====
select meter_id, local_date, count() as n
from {{ ref('daily_consumption') }}
group by meter_id, local_date
having n > 1

-- ===== then run =====
-- docker compose run --rm dbt test

exercises.title: Incremental model for late data
exercises.task: Rebuilding everything every night won't scale to billions of rows. Change stg_readings to an incremental model: ReplacingMergeTree(ingested_at), the append strategy, and on incremental runs only the rows whose loaded_at is newer than the latest one already in the model, minus a 1-hour safety overlap. Keep loaded_at as a column. Because the model now has duplicates until merges run, change daily_consumption to read {{ ref('stg_readings') }} … FINAL. Run dbt run --select stg_readings --full-refresh once, then dbt build. Run the check query and paste its result. Also compare SELECT count() FROM analytics.stg_readings with and without FINAL. In a real project the mart would be incremental too, rebuilding only the local dates that new rows touch (for example with the delete+insert or insert_overwrite strategy); ask your team which one they use.
exercises.hint: {% if is_incremental() %} where loaded_at > (select max(loaded_at) - interval 1 hour from {{ this }}) {% endif %}. Filter on loaded_at, not ts: a reading measured last week can arrive today.
exercises.verify:
SELECT
    (SELECT count() FROM analytics.stg_readings FINAL) AS stg_rows,
    (SELECT round(sum(consumption), 2) FROM analytics.daily_consumption) AS daily_total
exercises.solution:
-- ===== file: dbt/meter_project/models/staging/stg_readings.sql =====
{{ config(
    materialized         = 'incremental',
    incremental_strategy = 'append',
    engine               = 'ReplacingMergeTree(ingested_at)',
    order_by             = '(meter_id, ts)',
    partition_by         = 'toYYYYMM(ts)'
) }}

-- Incremental: each run only reads rows that reached lake.readings_raw since the last run.
-- We filter on loaded_at (when WE received the row), not on ts (when it was measured),
-- so late readings and corrections are always picked up. The 1-hour overlap is safe because
-- ReplacingMergeTree(ingested_at) keeps only the newest version of each (meter_id, ts).
select meter_id, ts, value, ingested_at, loaded_at
from {{ source('lake', 'readings_raw') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
where loaded_at > (select max(loaded_at) - interval 1 hour from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

-- ===== file: dbt/meter_project/models/marts/daily_consumption.sql =====
{{ config(
    materialized = 'table',
    engine       = 'MergeTree',
    order_by     = '(meter_id, local_date)'
) }}

with
    meters as (
        select meter_id, toDateTime(install_date, 'UTC') as installed_at
        from {{ ref('stg_meters') }}
    ),
    flagged as (
        select
            r.meter_id, r.ts, r.value,
            leadInFrame(r.value) over w as next_value,
            leadInFrame(r.ts)    over w as next_ts,
            row_number()         over w as rn,
            count()              over w as cnt
        from {{ ref('stg_readings') }} as r final   -- FINAL: read the deduplicated version
        window w as (partition by r.meter_id order by r.ts rows between unbounded preceding and unbounded following)
    ),
    clean as (   -- drop glitches: higher than the next reading, unless the next one is a replacement
        select f.meter_id, f.ts, f.value
        from flagged as f
        inner join meters as m on m.meter_id = f.meter_id
        where not (f.rn < f.cnt and f.value > f.next_value
                   and not (f.ts < m.installed_at and f.next_ts >= m.installed_at))
    ),
    deltas as (
        select
            meter_id, ts, value,
            lagInFrame(value) over w as prev_value,
            lagInFrame(ts)    over w as prev_ts,
            row_number()      over w as rn
        from clean
        window w as (partition by meter_id order by ts)
    )
select
    d.meter_id                           as meter_id,
    toDate(d.ts, 'Europe/Sarajevo')      as local_date,
    sum(if(d.prev_ts < m.installed_at and d.ts >= m.installed_at,
           d.value,                      -- first reading of a new meter counts from 0
           d.value - d.prev_value))      as consumption
from deltas as d
inner join meters as m on m.meter_id = d.meter_id
where d.rn > 1
group by d.meter_id, local_date

-- ===== then run =====
-- docker compose run --rm dbt run --select stg_readings --full-refresh
-- docker compose run --rm dbt build

-- ===== check query =====
SELECT
    (SELECT count() FROM analytics.stg_readings FINAL) AS stg_rows,
    (SELECT round(sum(consumption), 2) FROM analytics.daily_consumption) AS daily_total
